drafts.abstract: Sequence models still trade language capability against inference efficiency: attention becomes expensive as context grows, whereas recurrent alternatives may struggle with state tracking, retrieval, or hardware utilization. State-space models are appealing because they compress history into a fixed recurrent state and process sequences linearly, but this compact interface must support both expressive dynamics and efficient decoding. We present Mamba-3, an inference-oriented state-space architecture. Its mixer couples exponential-trapezoidal recurrence and learned trap interpolation with data-dependent complex rotations and multi-input multi-output projections, within a Llama-style stack using SwiGLU and normalized, biased B/C terms. The multi-input multi-output formulation raises arithmetic intensity under memory-bound decoding, while a fused single-input single-output path targets lower latency; both rely on specialized accelerator kernels. We evaluate matched model scales under common FineWeb-Edu pretraining, downstream language benchmarks, real and synthetic retrieval, formal state-tracking tasks, and accelerator kernel and end-to-end latency, comparing Transformers, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet. Mamba-3 delivers better language-model quality, downstream performance, formal state tracking, and recurrent decoding than the principal baselines. The architecture nevertheless presents a quality–speed choice between its multi-input multi-output and single-input single-output variants, while fixed-state recurrence can miss sparse facts and hybrid attention recovers retrieval only by reintroducing attention cost. Mamba-3 therefore offers a credible efficient sequence backbone, with larger-scale transfer, retrieval robustness, and kernel portability still requiring validation.

Strong language models still force an uncomfortable choice between Transformer quality and efficient recurrent inference, because attention costs grow with context while many linear models lose capability. State-space models process sequences with a fixed recurrent state, making them attractive for long-context serving, yet state expressivity and hardware utilization remain central obstacles. We present Mamba-3, an inference-first state-space model that addresses both obstacles. Its mixer combines an exponential-trapezoidal recurrence with a learned trap gate, data-dependent complex rotations, and a rank-4 MIMO state-space path inside a Llama-style stack. The MIMO path raises arithmetic intensity for memory-bound decoding, whereas fused SISO kernels target minimum latency. Evaluation covers shared 100B-token pretraining from 180M through 1.5B parameters, downstream language tasks, real and synthetic retrieval, formal state tracking, and H100 latency, with Transformer, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet baselines. Mamba-3 yields stronger modeling accuracy and state tracking together with faster recurrent decoding, but pure fixed-state models remain mixed on sparse-fact retrieval. At 1.5B, MIMO records 10.24 perplexity and 57.6 average accuracy, while SISO reaches 0.156 ms per token in the BF16, state-size-128 kernel setting. The variants therefore occupy distinct quality–latency points, and hybrid attention improves retrieval while restoring some attention cost. Overall, Mamba-3 is a compelling efficient backbone, although evidence beyond 1.5B and portability beyond specialized CUDA kernels remain open.

Transformer-quality sequence modeling remains difficult to reconcile with efficient long-context inference: attention incurs quadratic prefill and expanding cache costs, whereas recurrent alternatives can sacrifice accuracy and state tracking. We introduce Mamba-3, a state-space model designed to narrow this quality–efficiency gap. Mamba-3 uses an exponential-trapezoidal recurrence with a learned trap gate, data-dependent complex state rotations, and SISO or rank-4 MIMO projections, embedded in a Llama-style stack with SwiGLU and normalized B/C terms. We test matched models from 180M to 1.5B parameters trained on 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, then evaluate language modeling, downstream tasks, retrieval, formal state tracking, and H100 inference against Transformers, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet. The model improves perplexity, downstream accuracy, formal-state performance, and recurrent decode latency, while its pure recurrent form remains inconsistent on demanding semi-structured and unstructured retrieval. At 1.5B, MIMO reaches 10.24 perplexity and 57.6 average accuracy; on formal arithmetic with brackets, Mamba-3 scores 87.75 compared with 0.88 for Mamba-2. These gains indicate that richer recurrent dynamics can improve capability without abandoning efficient state-space processing, but fixed-state compression still risks losing sparse evidence and hybrid attention adds cost. Mamba-3 consequently provides a strong, released basis for efficient sequence modeling, with conclusions bounded by the reported 1.5B scale and specialized kernel requirements.

Transformer language models deliver strong quality, but quadratic attention, growing KV caches, and the weaker capability of many linear alternatives leave a persistent quality–efficiency gap. We introduce Mamba-3, an inference-oriented state-space sequence model designed to close this gap. It replaces simpler updates with an exponential-trapezoidal recurrence and learned trap gate, adds data-dependent complex rotations for richer state dynamics, and supports a rank-4 multi-input multi-output formulation. The resulting Llama-style stack combines the recurrent mixer with SwiGLU blocks, normalized and biased B/C projections, and fused implementations. MIMO increases arithmetic intensity in memory-bound decoding, while SISO provides the leanest latency point. We evaluate models from 180M to 1.5B parameters after shared 100B-token FineWeb-Edu pretraining, alongside retrieval, formal state-tracking, and H100 inference tests against Transformers, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet. Mamba-3 improves language-model quality, formal state tracking, and BF16 recurrent decoding, although pure recurrence remains uneven on difficult retrieval. At 1.5B, MIMO attains 10.24 perplexity and 57.6 average accuracy; at BF16 state size 128, SISO takes 0.156 ms per token versus 0.203 for Mamba-2. These results expose a practical tradeoff: MIMO favors quality, SISO favors speed, and hybrid attention can recover sparse-fact retrieval at added attention cost. Thus, Mamba-3 offers a promising efficient sequence backbone, with evidence currently bounded to models no larger than 1.5B and specialized GPU kernels.

Efficient long-context sequence modeling remains unresolved: Transformer attention carries growing compute and cache costs, but linear recurrent models can lose accuracy, state-tracking ability, or sparse evidence. State-space models offer linear sequence processing with a fixed recurrent state, so their usefulness depends on making that state expressive enough for language while preserving practical inference. We introduce Mamba-3, a new state-space architecture for this setting. It combines exponential-trapezoidal recurrence and learned trap interpolation, data-dependent complex rotations, and SISO or rank-4 MIMO projections in a Llama-style stack with SwiGLU and normalized, biased B/C terms. We compare matched models from 180M to 1.5B parameters trained on 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, and assess downstream language tasks, real and synthetic retrieval, formal state tracking, plus H100 kernel and end-to-end latency against Transformers, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet. Mamba-3 improves perplexity, average task accuracy, formal-state performance, and recurrent decode latency, though pure recurrence remains mixed on difficult retrieval. At 1.5B, MIMO obtains 10.24 perplexity and 57.6 average accuracy, versus 10.47 and 55.7 for Mamba-2; Mamba-3 also reaches 87.75 on bracketed arithmetic versus 0.88 for Mamba-2. The results favor richer state dynamics, but expose a retrieval tradeoff that hybrid attention mitigates at additional cost. Thus, Mamba-3 is a strong efficient backbone whose current evidence stops at 1.5B and specialized GPU implementations.

High-quality sequence models face a persistent deployment gap: Transformer attention becomes costly at long context, while efficient recurrent alternatives often trail in capability or underuse modern accelerators. We introduce Mamba-3, a state-space sequence model built to improve both modeling quality and inference behavior. Its architecture combines an exponential-trapezoidal recurrence and learned trap interpolation with data-dependent complex rotations and multi-input multi-output state-space projections, all within a Llama-style stack using SwiGLU and normalized B/C terms. The multi-input multi-output path increases arithmetic intensity during memory-bound decoding, while fused single-input single-output execution offers a faster operating point; specialized kernels realize both paths. We evaluate controlled, matched model scales under shared FineWeb-Edu pretraining, followed by downstream language benchmarks, real and synthetic retrieval, formal state-tracking tasks, and accelerator-level kernel and end-to-end latency tests against Transformers, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet. Across these settings, Mamba-3 improves language modeling, downstream accuracy, formal state tracking, and recurrent decoding efficiency. However, the quality-oriented multi-input multi-output variant is not always the fastest, and pure fixed-state recurrence remains uneven when retrieval requires retaining many sparse facts; hybrid attention helps but restores attention costs. The evidence therefore supports Mamba-3 as a practical quality–efficiency architecture, while leaving larger-scale transfer, difficult retrieval, and hardware portability as bounded follow-up questions.
